clinicalPearls: Rare intraepithelial adenocarcinoma of apocrine gland-bearing skin, most often the vulva, and also the perineum, perianal skin, scrotum, penis and axilla.
Presents as a chronic, well-demarcated erythematous and eczematous or 'strawberries-and-cream' plaque with itch or burning, frequently misdiagnosed as eczema or dermatophyte infection for years.
Classified as primary (intraepidermal cutaneous adenocarcinoma) or secondary (epidermotropic spread from an underlying or adjacent adnexal, anorectal, urothelial or other visceral adenocarcinoma).
Perianal and penoscrotal disease carry a higher association with underlying malignancy and warrant directed screening.
Histology shows large pale Paget cells with abundant cytoplasm scattered within the epidermis, positive for mucin stains and cytokeratin 7.
Immunoprofile aids origin: GCDFP-15 favours primary cutaneous disease, CK20 and CDX2 suggest anorectal origin, and uroplakin or GATA3 point to urothelial origin.
Wide local excision, often with Mohs micrographic surgery, is the mainstay, but subclinical multifocal extension leads to frequent positive margins and recurrence.
Any dermal nodule or induration suggests invasion and should prompt an adequate-depth biopsy and staging.
reference.pathophysiology: Extramammary Paget disease is an intraepidermal proliferation of malignant glandular (Paget) cells. Primary disease is thought to arise from intraepidermal apocrine or eccrine ductal cells or Toker cell precursors as an adenocarcinoma in situ that may progress to dermal invasion. Secondary disease represents pagetoid epidermotropic spread from an underlying regional adenocarcinoma, such as anorectal or urothelial carcinoma. The neoplastic cells characteristically produce mucin and express cytokeratin 7, and their broader immunohistochemical profile helps distinguish primary from secondary disease and identify the underlying source.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic eczema or allergic contact dermatitis
Bowen disease (squamous cell carcinoma in situ)
additionalInvestigations: Full-thickness or punch skin biopsy with immunohistochemistry (CK7, CK20, GCDFP-15, CDX2, GATA3, uroplakin, HER2, S100/melan-A)
Examination of all apocrine-bearing sites and palpation of regional lymph nodes
Colonoscopy and anorectal examination for perianal disease
Cystoscopy and urine cytology for penoscrotal or periurethral disease
Gynaecological examination and pelvic imaging for vulval disease
Cross-sectional imaging (CT, MRI or PET) where invasive or nodal disease is suspected
Breast examination and mammography, and HER2 testing to inform systemic therapy, where indicated
redFlags: Palpable dermal nodule or induration suggesting invasive disease
Symptoms of an associated visceral adenocarcinoma such as rectal bleeding or haematuria
Rapid enlargement, ulceration or bleeding of the plaque
Persistent anogenital 'eczema' unresponsive to appropriate topical therapy
reference.prognosis: Non-invasive primary disease has a good prognosis but a high rate of local recurrence owing to subclinical spread. Dermal invasion, nodal involvement or an associated internal malignancy markedly worsen the outlook.
pitfalls: Prolonged empirical treatment as eczema or fungal infection, delaying diagnostic biopsy
Failing to screen for an underlying malignancy in perianal or penoscrotal disease
Accepting positive surgical margins from subclinical extension, leading to recurrence
Missing dermal invasion because of an inadequate-depth biopsy
Misinterpreting pagetoid cells as melanoma without a confirmatory immunohistochemistry panel
management: Determine two things before treatment: whether disease is confined to the epidermis (in situ) or has invaded the dermis, and whether it is primary cutaneous disease or secondary to an underlying visceral adenocarcinoma.

Surgical excision is the mainstay for in situ (curative-intent) disease; because EMPD spreads subclinically and is often multifocal, margins are frequently positive even after apparently adequate excision, driving local recurrence.
For extensive or surgically difficult in situ disease in patients who are poor surgical candidates, non-surgical local options include topical imiquimod, radiotherapy, or photodynamic therapy.
Mohs micrographic surgery is an alternative excisional technique with lower reported local recurrence where the expertise is available.

Once dermal invasion or nodal disease is present, treat as invasive adenocarcinoma of the site rather than an in-situ lesion; surgery remains the cornerstone, with radiotherapy or systemic chemotherapy considered as adjuncts for locally advanced, node-positive, or margin-positive disease.

Systemic therapy is reserved for invasive, nodal, or metastatic disease, or for an underlying secondary adenocarcinoma, and follows the site-specific pathway for that associated cancer rather than a distinct EMPD regimen.

For secondary EMPD (epidermotropic spread from an underlying anorectal, urothelial, or other visceral adenocarcinoma), manage the skin surgically but treat the underlying primary according to its own site-specific staging and treatment pathway.

All patients should undergo colonoscopy and appropriate genitourinary malignancy screening before treatment to rule out an internal malignancy and secondary EMPD, with site-specific evaluation extended as appropriate (e.g. urothelial evaluation for penoscrotal disease, gynaecologic evaluation for vulval disease).
Any new nodule, induration, ulceration, or growth in a previously treated or observed area should prompt re-biopsy to reassess for dermal invasion.
Long-term surveillance is required after treatment given high local recurrence rates, driven by the subclinical multifocal nature of the disease rather than true relapse from a new primary.

Refer to a multidisciplinary team spanning dermato-oncology or dermatologic surgery, surgical oncology, and the relevant site specialist (colorectal surgery, urology, or gynaecologic oncology depending on site), since the surgical approach and the search for an underlying malignancy are intertwined.

Refer for radiation oncology and medical oncology input once dermal invasion, nodal involvement, or an associated invasive visceral adenocarcinoma is identified, since management then follows the invasive-cancer pathway of the relevant primary site.
